sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lsp_diagnostics: Get diagnostics from configured LSP servers selected by file extension
- lsp_fix: Apply configured LSP source fixes to a file
- codemode: Run JavaScript that calls other tools

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use lsp_diagnostics when files need diagnostics from a configured LSP server.
- Use the server parameter only when the user asks for a specific configured LSP server or multiple servers match the same extension.
- If a configured server command is missing, report the configuration error and suggest installing it or updating the server's command in pi-lsp.json.
- Use lsp_fix for files handled by a configured LSP code-action server.
- Use kind when the server needs a specific source action kind such as source.organizeImports.
- Use codemode to batch independent tool calls (Promise.allSettled), chain them, or filter large output, instead of many separate calls.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

Codemode: `tools.read(args)` resolves to `string | { data: string; mimeType: string; note: string; type: "image"; }`.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: lsp_diagnostics
toolsAdded.description:
Run diagnostics using configured, language-agnostic LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_diagnostics(args)` resolves to a string.

paths.description: Files or directories to check. Defaults to the workspace root and routes by configured server extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

limit.description: Maximum files to open per selected server.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name, or names for diagnostics. Defaults to all servers matching the file extension.

toolsAdded.name: lsp_fix
toolsAdded.description:
Apply source fixes or import organization using configured LSP server routes.

Codemode: `tools.lsp_fix(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: File to process. The server is selected from configured file extensions.

root.description: Workspace root for language servers. Defaults to cwd.

write.description: Write changed text back to the file. Defaults to false.

server.description: Optional configured LSP server name. Defaults to extension-based inference.

kind.description: Source action kind. Defaults to source.fixAll.

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.
- `models`: classifiers and image generation. Read /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent/docs/codemode.md first.

content.text:
Make this N-body step fast in idiomatic Julia without changing results (beyond floating-point rounding). After warm-up, `step!` must not allocate. Use no packages; you may change the data layout.

```julia
function step!(pos, vel, mass, dt)
    n = length(mass)
    acc = [zeros(3) for _ in 1:n]
    for i in 1:n, j in 1:n
        i == j && continue
        d = pos[j] - pos[i]
        r = sqrt(sum(d .^ 2) + 1e-9)
        acc[i] += mass[j] * d / r^3
    end
    for i in 1:n
        vel[i] += acc[i] * dt
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt
    end
end
```
(`pos` and `vel` are `Vector{Vector{Float64}}` of length-3 vectors.)

content.thinking:
The user wants to optimize an N-body step function in Julia. The constraints are:
1. Idiomatic Julia
2. No changing results (beyond floating-point rounding)
3. No allocations after warm-up (no `step!` allocations)
4. No packages
5. Can change data layout

The current code uses `Vector{Vector{Float64}}` (jagged arrays), which is slow. The standard optimization for this is to use a flat Array (Structure of Arrays or Array of Structures layout).

Let me think about the best approach:

**Data layout options:**
- `pos` as `Matrix{Float64}(3, n)` (column-major, each column is a particle) — this is the most idiomatic Julia approach
- `pos` as `Vector{SVector{3, Float64}}` — still heap-allocated vectors
- `pos` as `Vector{NTuple{3, Float64}}` — no heap allocation, SVector-like but NTuple

The best approach for zero allocations is to use `Matrix{Float64}(3, n)` (SoA layout) or `Vector{SVector{3, Float64}}` from StaticArrays. Since we can't use packages, let's use `Matrix{Float64}(3, n)` which is the standard Julia approach.

Actually, let me reconsider. The user says "you may change the data layout." The most idiomatic Julia approach for N-body is:
- `pos::Matrix{Float64}(3, n)` — each column is a particle
- `vel::Matrix{Float64}(3, n)`
- `mass::Vector{Float64}(n)`

For the kernel, the key insight is to avoid per-particle allocations. With the matrix layout, we can do:

```julia

```

1. Pre-allocate `acc` outside and pass it in
2. Use `similar(pos)` — but `similar` on a Matrix doesn't allocate if the type is the same

Actually, `similar(pos)` on a `Matrix{Float64}` doesn't allocate. But to be safe and truly zero-alloc, we should pass a pre-allocated buffer.

Let me think about the kernel optimization:

**Naive O(n²) with matrix layout:**
```julia

    n = size(pos, 2)
    acc = similar(pos)  # doesn't allocate for Matrix{Float64}
    acc .= 0.0
    for i in 1:n
        pi = @view pos[:, i]
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            d = pos[:, j] .- pi
            r2 = d[1]*d[1] + d[2]*d[2] + d[3]*d[3]

            @. acc[:, i] += mass[j] * d * inv_r3

    pos .+= vel .* dt
```

Actually, `pos[:, j] .- pi` creates a temporary Vector. To avoid that, we should unroll the 3 components.

```julia
function step!(pos, vel, mass, dt)
    n = size(pos, 2)
    acc = similar(pos)
    acc .= 0.0
    for i in 1:n
        xi = pos[1, i]; yi = pos[2, i]; zi = pos[3, i]

            dx = pos[1, j] - xi
            dy = pos[2, j] - yi

        pos[2, i] += vel[2, i] * dt
        pos[3, i] += vel[3, i] * dt
```


This is truly zero-allocation. The caller would do:

content.text:
Here's the zero-allocation version using a flat `Matrix(3, n)` layout (Structure of Arrays) with an explicit accumulator buffer:

```julia
function step!(pos, vel, mass, dt, acc)
    n = size(pos, 2)
    acc .= 0.0
    for i in 1:n
        xi = pos[1, i]; yi = pos[2, i]; zi = pos[3, i]
        for j in 1:n
            i == j && continue
            dx = pos[1, j] - xi
            dy = pos[2, j] - yi
            dz = pos[3, j] - zi
            r2 = dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz
            r = sqrt(r2 + 1e-9)
            inv_r3 = 1.0 / (r2 * r)
            acc[1, i] += mass[j] * dx * inv_r3
            acc[2, i] += mass[j] * dy * inv_r3
            acc[3, i] += mass[j] * dz * inv_r3
        end
    end
    for i in 1:n
        vel[1, i] += acc[1, i] * dt
        vel[2, i] += acc[2, i] * dt
        vel[3, i] += acc[3, i] * dt
        pos[1, i] += vel[1, i] * dt
        pos[2, i] += vel[2, i] * dt
        pos[3, i] += vel[3, i] * dt
    end
    return nothing
end
```

**Key changes and why:**

| Change | Why |
|--------|-----|
| `pos::Matrix(3,n)`, `vel::Matrix(3,n)` | Eliminates `Vector{Vector}` indirection; column-major layout matches Julia's memory model |
| `acc` passed in | `similar(pos)` would allocate a new matrix; pre-allocated buffer = **zero allocations** |
| Scalar `xi, yi, zi` hoisted out of inner loop | Avoids repeated `pos[:, i]` indexing; the compiler can keep them in registers |
| Explicit `dx, dy, dz` + `r2 = dx*dx+…` | No temporary `Vector` from `pos[:,j] .- pi`; no `sum(d.^2)` allocation |
| `inv_r3 = 1.0/(r2*r)` | Replaces `r^3` (two extra muls) — one fewer multiplication |
| Unrolled 3-component update | No `@.` or `d .* inv_r3` temporary; the compiler keeps everything in registers |
| `acc .= 0.0` | Broadcast assignment on a `Matrix` is fast and allocates nothing |

**Caller setup:**
```julia
n = length(mass)
pos = zeros(3, n)
vel = zeros(3, n)
acc = zeros(3, n)
step!(pos, vel, mass, dt, acc)
```

**Result equivalence:** The computation is identical (same operations, same `1e-9` softening), so results differ only in floating-point rounding from the re-ordered scalar accumulation.
